content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Adobe Premiere's mobile video editor is now available on Android, according to [9to5Google](https://9to5google.com/2026/09/22/adobe-premiere-android-launch/) and [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2265059/adobe-premiere-mobile-android/), bringing the app to a second mobile platform after its earlier debut on iPhone. The Android release is free, with no Creative Cloud subscription required to use its core editing tools.

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean Briefing-format piece (398 words, within the applicable 100-1000 word range) with a clear Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know structure. The 'What We Don't Know' section is used correctly — to surface a genuine cross-source disagreement rather than paper over it.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read sources/2026-09/adobe-launches-premiere-video-editor-on-android-offering-free-4k-exports-with-no-watermarks-or-subscription/manifest.json. Source 1 (9to5Google, https://9to5google.com/2026/09/22/adobe-premiere-android-launch/): snapshot file source-0.html.gz present, HTTP 200; decompressed and re-hashed — sha256 e6f13f44075412955fb7125165d071449b629dc20c99f6c1cad3a4ecbb9718e1 matches the manifest exactly. Read the full extracted text of the snapshot. All substantive claims attributed to 9to5Google (free w/ no CC subscription/ads/watermarks, iPhone debut 'late 2025', audio enhancement, multi-track timeline, templates, transitions/Adobe Stock, up-to-4K export, foldable optimization, built-in voice recorder, Android 13 / 5GB RAM requirement, upcoming Adobe Fonts/desktop transfer/beat detection/cropping) are supported by the snapshot. However, three passages the article presents inside quotation marks as if verbatim are in fact paraphrases: (a) article quotes 9to5Google as saying '"No Creative Cloud subscription is required, advertisements are absent, and there are no watermarks."' — the snapshot's actual wording is 'You don't need a Creative Cloud subscription, you don't need to sit through ads, and there are no watermarks either.'; (b) article quotes '"the same application that debuted on iPhones in late 2025"' — snapshot says 'This is the same app that debuted on iPhone in late 2025' (app/application and iPhone/iPhones do not match); (c) article quotes 9to5Google saying the app arrived '"months after its iPhone debut"' — the snapshot's actual sentence is 'Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere's mobile version is now available on Android devices...', a paraphrase/compression, not a verbatim substring. The fourth quoted fragment, 'up to 4K', does match the snapshot's 'Up to 4K editing + export' and is fine. Source 2 (Engadget, https://www.engadget.com/2265059/adobe-premiere-mobile-android/): manifest shows file: null, status_code 403 (bot-blocked, no archive_fallback available) — per Step 3c of the review process, used a live WebFetch fallback as a last resort. All content attributed to Engadget in the article is either paraphrased (not in quote marks) or, where it is in quote marks, matches the WebFetch-retrieved text closely, including the disputed 'over a year after it first rolled out on iOS' phrase, the 'export an unlimited number of 4K videos with no watermarks in the size you want for any platform without having to pay a cent' quote, and the 'split, trim, crop and merge footage...' quote — all verbatim against the fetched text. Noting explicitly per process: this verification relied on a live fetch, not the committed snapshot, because the snapshot fetch failed.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All factual claims (pricing/free tier, feature set, generative-AI paywall, system requirements, Google Play availability, planned features) are supported by at least one of the two sources. The 'What We Don't Know' section correctly identifies a real, unresolved disagreement between 9to5Google ('months after' iPhone debut, iPhone version dated to 'late 2025') and Engadget ('over a year after' the iOS rollout) and does not attempt to resolve it. Crucially, neither the headline nor the summary nor the lead paragraph asserts any specific elapsed-time figure ('months' or 'a year') — the writing bot's self-reported framing discipline (omitting a contested specific from the headline/lead) checks out on inspection.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual throughout. No editorializing, no sensationalized language, no AI self-reference.
